questions.stem: A patient with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction asks whether furosemide will help them live longer. What is the best answer?

options.text: Yes, it is one of the four pillars
No, it eases breathing but does not help patients live longer

questions.explanation: D is correct: loop diuretics like furosemide remove fluid and ease breathing, but they do not help patients live longer. A is wrong because furosemide is not a pillar. B is wrong because higher doses add fluid loss, not survival; the goal is the lowest dose that keeps the patient dry. C is wrong because digoxin does not lower death either.

questions.stem: Which ejection fraction meets the definition of reduced ejection fraction?
questions.explanation: C is correct: an ejection fraction of 40% or less is reduced, and 38% is below 40%. A, B, and D are all above 40%.

questions.stem: Which drugs are part of the four pillars for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: B, C, E, and F are correct: the pillars are sacubitril-valsartan, a proven beta-blocker like carvedilol, a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist like spironolactone, and a sodium-glucose cotransporter two inhibitor like dapagliflozin. A, furosemide, eases congestion but does not help patients live longer. D, digoxin, can reduce hospital stays but does not lower death.

questions.stem: Which beta-blocker is proven in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction?
questions.explanation: C is correct: only carvedilol, metoprolol succinate, and bisoprolol are proven. A, metoprolol tartrate, is the short-acting form and is not proven. B, atenolol, and D, propranolol, are not among the three proven beta-blockers.

questions.stem: A patient with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction takes metoprolol tartrate twice daily. What should the pharmacist recommend?
questions.explanation: B is correct: metoprolol succinate, the long-acting form, is proven; metoprolol tartrate is a different product and is not proven. A keeps an unproven product. C switches to a beta-blocker that is not among the three proven ones. D removes a pillar that helps patients live longer.

questions.stem: A patient with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction has potassium 5.3 mEq/L and an estimated kidney filtration rate of 50. Should spironolactone be started now?

options.text: No, potassium must be below 5.0 first

questions.explanation: A is correct: start a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist only if potassium is below 5 and kidney filtration is above 30; 5.3 fails the potassium rule. B is wrong because both rules must be met, not just filtration. C makes high potassium more likely. D adds more potassium to a level that is already high.

questions.stem: Spironolactone was just started. When should potassium and kidney function be rechecked?

options.text: Only if the patient feels palpitations

questions.explanation: A is correct: recheck potassium and kidney function within a week, then regularly. B and C wait too long to catch rising potassium. D waits for symptoms, but high potassium can cause dangerous heart rhythms first.

questions.stem: Which drugs can make heart failure with reduced ejection fraction worse? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: B, C, D, E, and F are correct: ibuprofen and naproxen hold salt and water, diltiazem and verapamil weaken the squeeze, and pioglitazone causes fluid retention. A, dapagliflozin, is one of the four pillars and helps.

questions.stem: A patient with reduced ejection fraction takes sacubitril-valsartan, metoprolol succinate, spironolactone, and furosemide. Which addition lowers the risk of death?
questions.explanation: C is correct: dapagliflozin completes the fourth pillar. A, digoxin, can reduce hospital stays but does not lower death. B, diltiazem, worsens heart failure. D, metoprolol tartrate, is not the proven form, and the patient already takes a proven beta-blocker.

questions.stem: Why are diltiazem and verapamil avoided in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction?
questions.explanation: A is correct: diltiazem and verapamil weaken the squeeze. B describes mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists like spironolactone. C is a side effect of the sodium-glucose drugs. D describes sacubitril.
